video_title: Why Distributed Transactions Can't Be ACID
core_insight: ACID guarantees break at network boundaries; you can’t hold locks across services, so you must trade immediate atomicity for local transactions with compensations.

scenes.voice: If you have two accounts in different services, can you still do an all-or-nothing transfer?
scenes.visual: Two service boxes with separate databases, an arrow trying to wrap both in one box labeled ACID.

scenes.voice: A single database gives you atomicity: debit A and credit B both happen or neither happens. That works because there is one log and one lock manager.
scenes.visual: Single DB with one transaction box covering two rows, check mark.

scenes.voice: Put the accounts in different services and you cross a network. No shared lock manager, no single log, and the network can partition or delay.
scenes.visual: Network line between services, lock icon broken in middle.

scenes.voice: The obvious fix is 2PC: coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then commit or abort. It gives strong atomicity but locks resources until decision and needs everyone available.
scenes.visual: Coordinator box with prepare/commit arrows to two participants.

scenes.voice: In microservices that is a distributed lock and a single point of failure. The practical way is to make each step a local transaction and define a compensation.
scenes.visual: Three steps in a row, each with a local commit check, and a reverse arrow labeled compensate.

scenes.voice: That is a Saga. Orchestrator runs reserve inventory, charge payment, schedule shipping. If payment fails, it triggers release reservation. Services stay autonomous.
scenes.visual: Sequence diagram of orchestrator to inventory, payment, shipping with compensation note.
scenes.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Orchestrator
    participant Inventory
    participant Payment
    participant Shipping
    Orchestrator->>Inventory: reserve items
    Inventory-->>Orchestrator: reserved
    Orchestrator->>Payment: charge card
    Payment-->>Orchestrator: charged
    Orchestrator->>Shipping: schedule
    Shipping-->>Orchestrator: scheduled
    Note over Orchestrator,Shipping: If payment fails -> compensate inventory
    Orchestrator->>Inventory: release reservation

scenes.voice: You gain availability and autonomy, you sacrifice immediate consistency. Design for idempotent steps and reliable outbox delivery, not distributed locks.
scenes.visual: Scale up icon vs clock icon, trade-off balance.

mental_model: Think of distributed transactions as coordinating independent actors who each commit locally. Choose all-or-nothing now with coordination cost, or all-or-nothing eventually with local transactions plus compensations.
final_takeaway: ACID does not cross network boundaries for free. Use local transactions with compensations when availability matters more than immediate atomicity.
